title: AI Platform Engineering: Patrick Debois
talk_summary: Patrick Debois applies DevOps/team-topologies history to AI platform engineering: centralize model access, RAG/connectors, model registry, a proxy for access control, observability/tracing, evals-as-monitoring, caching and feedback-as-a-service, then enable teams on top. He also warns that AI-generated code increases review load and erodes situational awareness, and that model churn forces costly prompt rework without evals.

takeaways.technique: Central model-access proxy with access control
takeaways.what_they_do: A platform team picks approved models and puts a proxy in front so not every team goes out and uses whatever model they want; also standardizes on the OpenAI protocol for provider-agnosticism.
takeaways.evidence_quote: there's like a proxy that these kind of environments are building uh so not everybody can just go out and use whatever they want

takeaways.technique: Evals as production health checks before model swaps
takeaways.what_they_do: They went through ~8 LLMs in two years and each swap required manually reworking prompts with no guarantee it worked; he argues you need testing evals before refactoring, and evals running continuously in production like health checks.
takeaways.evidence_quote: every time we change the model we have to rewrite and rework all the application prompts ... they were doing this manually so I had no guarantee
takeaways.numbers: eight different models over two years

takeaways.technique: Treat AI review as the new bottleneck, not free throughput
takeaways.what_they_do: Copilot increased code volume but review times went up and AI-authored PRs were bigger; the human shifts from producer to reviewer and loses situational awareness, leading to rubber-stamping.
takeaways.evidence_quote: review times went up and the PRS sent by the actual AI were bigger right so we got faster but then we started slowing down again

takeaways.technique: Platform-team abstraction over shared AI services
takeaways.what_they_do: Instead of every feature team rebuilding RAG, connectors, model registry, caching, feedback, observability, one platform team provides them as services with enablement on top.
takeaways.evidence_quote: instead of have them having to do this all the time one by one on teams and figuring out how that works

takeaways.technique: Caching and feedback as centralized services
takeaways.what_they_do: Caching services and feedback-as-a-service (thumbs, inline edits) are called out as expensive to build per-team and better centrally managed; feedback beyond thumbs is richer signal.
takeaways.evidence_quote: you don't want every team to build this service because it's quite expensive uh and you want this to be centrally uh managed

takeaways.technique: Don't over-invest in platform before use cases are real
takeaways.what_they_do: Warns against 'every part of the product needs GenAI' and premature optimization; focus on the business case first, cost will fall as models get cheaper.
takeaways.evidence_quote: don't do premature optimization but if you're scaling out to 10 and more teams that's probably a pattern that is known
